title: A Poster on Data Justice in Remote Sensing
text:
Proud to have contributed to this poster on Data Justice in Remote Sensing, designed and illustrated by Larissa Lachmann and based on the work of Prof. Mia Bennett.
Satellite imagery often appears neutral, but it isn’t: decisions about who measures what, who controls the data, and who shapes the analysis all matter. The poster — an initial effort by the Earth Observation Lab at Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin — lays out where power imbalances show up in remote sensing research and offers concrete starting points for making our work more just, from checking our own data to structural change, education, and meaningful engagement with the communities we study.



“Can we make our research more just?” — poster concept by Lasse Harkort, design by Larissa Lachmann, conceptual foundation based on the work of Prof. Mia Bennett

title: Pixel Politics: Advancing Critical Remote Sensing
text:
Pixel Politics: Who owns the satellites—and the stories they tell? Today we had the pleasure of welcoming Prof. Mia Bennett (University of Washington) to our EO Lab colloquium. Prof. Bennett explores the geopolitics of infrastructure at the planet’s frontiers—from the Arctic to orbital space. Her work combines geospatial methods with critical and ethnographic approaches to reveal how technologies, power, and politics shape these spaces.
In her talk Pixel Politics: Advancing Critical Remote Sensing, she asked provocative questions: Who controls the satellites and their data? Who benefits—and who might be put at risk—when places are made visible? How can remote sensing move from exposure to true engagement and empowerment?
Her roadmap—Exposure → Engagement → Empowerment—invites us to rethink our own roles as scientists and to reflect on the politics of the pixels we analyze.



Prof. Mia Bennett presenting “Pixel Politics: Advancing Critical Remote Sensing” at the EO Lab colloquium

title: Presenting at the Living Planet Symposium 2025
text:
Excited to present at the Living Planet Symposium (LPS25) in Vienna on our novel phenology-based approach to mapping vegetation fractions in semi-arid Sub-Saharan rangelands. The framework helps characterize vegetation changes at landscape scale, including woody thickening and the impacts of extreme events on the resources people and animals depend on.

title: Young Scientist Award
text:
I am honored to have received the Young Scientists Award at the 14th EARSeL Workshop on Imaging Spectroscopy, hosted by Aalto University in Helsinki, Finland. Here I presented my recent research on “Capturing the Pulse of the Dry Season” showing how EnMAP hyperspectral data can be used to distinguish herbaceous from woody plant NPV types. I specifically want to thank my Co-Authors, the Earth Observation lab for their ongoing support and the Namibian Rangeland Farmers helping us to do the invaluable field work.



Receiving the Young Scientists Award at the EARSeL Workshop on Imaging Spectroscopy
